## Overview

This project describes how I use **engineering drawings** and **technical documentation** daily in **manufacturing production**. Drawings are the contract between design and production—every **kit cut**, **CNC operation**, and **inspection** traces back to a controlled revision on paper or PDF.

## Background of the Study

Advanced manufacturing depends on **lamination schedules** (ply order and orientation), **assembly drawings** (how parts fit together), and **detail drawings** (dimensions, tolerances, notes). Misreading a symbol or an old revision can scrap thousands of dollars in material. Structured drawing literacy is as important as machine skills.

## Motivation of the Study

- Prevent **revision errors** before cutting or machining  
- Communicate clearly with **engineering, QA, and layup** teams  
- Connect **IT/documentation habits** (version control mindset) to **shop travelers**  
- Support career growth across **manufacturing, quality, and technical leadership**  

## Tools & Documents

| Document | Typical use |
|----------|-------------|
| Assembly drawing | Overall part structure and interfaces |
| Detail / lamination drawing | Ply shapes, orientations, materials |
| Engineering notes block | Process specs, cure cycle references |
| Revision table | Current rev letter/number and change history |
| Job traveler | Sign-offs, lot numbers, operation sequence |
| GD&T feature control frames | Critical tolerances and datums |

## Step-by-Step Workflow

### Step 1 — Obtain controlled drawing

1. Pull drawing from **released document system** (not informal email copies).  
2. Record **revision letter/number** and **date** on the traveler.  
3. Confirm drawing **part number** matches work order.

### Step 2 — Read title block and notes

1. Identify **material specification**, **finish**, and **cure reference** in notes.  
2. Note **scale** (e.g., 1:1 on ply details, 1:5 on assembly).  
3. List **special process** requirements (autoclave vs. OOA, bagging, demold).

### Step 3 — Interpret lamination schedule

1. Read ply table: **ply number, material, orientation (0/45/90), sequence**.  
2. Match each ply to **cut nest ID** on kit cutting drawing.  
3. Flag **missing plies** or **ambiguous orientations** with engineering before layup.

### Step 4 — Extract dimensions for cutting and CNC

1. For kit cutting: verify **outline dimensions** and **fiber direction arrow**.  
2. For CNC: identify **datums**, **hole patterns**, and **profile tolerances**.  
3. Highlight **critical-to-quality (CTQ)** dimensions for extra inspection.

### Step 5 — Apply GD&T (as applicable)

1. Locate **datum feature symbols** (A, B, C).  
2. Read **position, flatness, profile** callouts on mating surfaces.  
3. If tolerance stack-up is unclear, request **engineering clarification** in writing.

### Step 6 — Cross-check with 3D/CAM (if used)

1. Compare drawing dimensions to **CAD model** revision.  
2. Resolve discrepancies **before** generating CAM or cut files.  
3. Save screenshot or redline for quality record if change issued.

### Step 7 — Document on traveler

1. List **operations completed** (cut, CNC, drill, deburr).  
2. Sign and **date** each operation per shop policy.  
3. Attach **FAI**, photos, or measurement sheets when required.

### Step 8 — Manage revisions

1. When new rev issued, **quarantine** old kits and obsolete programs.  
2. Re-cut or re-program only from **new rev** after approval.  
3. Update **setup sheets** and **program IDs** to match rev.

## Drawing Elements Reference

| Symbol / element | Meaning in practice |
|------------------|---------------------|
| Fiber direction arrow | Layup orientation on tool surface |
| Rev cloud / triangle | Changed area on drawing |
| ± tolerance | Acceptable dimensional band |
| Datum Ⓐ | Primary reference for setup and inspection |
| Section view A-A | Internal ply stack or core detail |
| Note flag | Mandatory process instruction |

## Quality Control & Safety

- **No manufacturing** from unmarked or “draft” drawings.  
- **Redlines** require engineering approval before production use.  
- **Measurement records** retained per traveler for audit trail.  
- **FOD:** Keep drawings clean and protected from oils and shop debris.  

## Outcomes & Skills Gained

- Confident **engineering drawing** interpretation for production builds  
- **Revision discipline** aligned with aerospace-style quality  
- Clear handoff between **documentation → kit cutting → CNC → layup**  
- Portfolio evidence of **manufacturing + technical communication** skills
